results.answer:
To claim a miss rate of **at most 1% at 95% confidence**, you need **299 independent encounters with zero misses—for each population you claim performance for**. Tightening the target to 0.1% requires 2,995; to 0.01%, 29,956. That makes statistical trial volume a major driver of the validation campaign, not just scenario coverage. [f220, f221, f222, f6654]

### Required trial counts

These are **one-sided confidence bounds**, assuming zero observed misses and independent trials. [f6653, f6876]

| Maximum miss rate claimed | Trials at 95% confidence | Trials at 99% confidence |
|---|---:|---:|
| 1% | **299** | 459 |
| 0.1% | **2,995** | 4,603 |
| 0.01% | **29,956** | 46,050 |

[f220, f221, f222, f6653]

The exact zero-miss calculation is \(n=\lceil\ln(\alpha)/\ln(1-q)\rceil\), where \(q\) is the maximum miss probability and \(\alpha\) is one minus the confidence level. [f6876] If misses occur, the zero-miss counts no longer apply: for a 1% claim at 95% confidence, the booklet gives approximately **474 trials with one allowed miss**, or **630 with two**. [f6879, f6880]

### What this means for the campaign

- **Define the claim before collecting data.** Fix the target miss rate, confidence level and population. These counts are statistical consequences of that claim—not sample sizes prescribed by a standard. [f14200, f14201]

- **Budget by critical stratum, not just total runs.** A 1% claim in each of 20 critical strata requires about **6,000 zero-miss encounters**, with 95% confidence for each stratum. Conversely, 2,995 runs sampled from one defined population support one aggregate 0.1% claim—not a blanket claim across an entire product family. [f6654, f6885]

- **Count encounters, not sensor frames.** A ten-second encounter yielding about 300 camera frames is still **one** independent encounter. Counting those frames as separate trials makes the confidence bound grossly overconfident. [f14195]

- **Keep failure discovery separate from performance estimation.** The booklet recommends separate discovery, estimation and requirement/regression campaigns. The rate claim should come from a frozen, pre-registered, stratified estimation sample; the failure fraction from an adversarial discovery campaign must not be presented as a field miss rate. [f6665, f6667, f6669]

- **Plan high-volume simulation/HIL with a credibility argument.** The booklet judges roughly 6,000 trials feasible only through simulation or hardware-in-the-loop, but low simulated miss rates require an accompanying credibility argument. It found no off-road precedent for regulatory or notified-body acceptance of simulation evidence for collision avoidance, and it did **not quantify** the compute/HIL throughput needed for this workload. [f6654, f6925, f7417, f7449]

- **Add a separate false-intervention exposure campaign.** Successful detection trials do not replace representative operating hours: under the zero-event Poisson calculation, **300 hours with no unnecessary braking** support a 95% upper bound below one unnecessary brake per 100 hours. [f6658]

Finally, an aggregate “real-world miss rate” needs defensible weighting across operating conditions. Without good field telemetry, the booklet says that weighting remains uncertain—even if individual strata have large test counts. [f7423]

results.answer:
**20 January 2027 is the immediate conformity deadline—not the later AI milestone.** For heavy off-road automatic braking, the booklet identifies a potential notified-body requirement where ML performs a safety function; its **2 August 2028** AI milestone does not remove the machinery obligations applying in 2027. [f2089, f2090, f2094]

## Dates and rules

- **9 December 2026 — Product Liability Directive (EU) 2024/2853.** The booklet says it applies to products placed on the market after this date, treats software as a product and permits court-ordered disclosure. This concerns liability and evidence, rather than a separate braking approval route. [f9461, f9462, f10451, f2009]
- **20 January 2027 — Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 applies.** Annex I Part A covers safety components with “fully or partially self-evolving behaviour using machine learning approaches ensuring safety functions,” and machinery embedding them. The listed routes—EU type-examination, unit verification or full quality assurance—involve a **notified body**. [f2089, f2090, f2205]
- **8 July / 27 July 2026 — reported AI amendment adoption / entry into force.** The booklet identifies Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, the *Digital Omnibus on AI*, as moving Annex I high-risk obligations to **2 August 2028** and directing machinery-specific AI requirements toward delegated acts under the Machinery Regulation. Those delegated requirements had **not been adopted by 1 October 2026**. [f2093, f2094, f2096, f2098]

**Important qualification:** the booklet is internally inconsistent about the AI route. Chapter 3 says machinery is removed from direct AI Act high-risk classification; Chapter 13 says the change is a deferral, not an exemption, with conformity required if the component qualifies. Chapter 12 also acknowledges reliance on secondary summaries for the detailed provisions. Treat the 2028 milestone as a planning constraint, but obtain primary-text/legal confirmation of the applicable route before committing to launch timing. [f2095, f11223, f11224, f10308]

## What ML changes

A **trained-then-frozen perception model is not a settled exemption**. Commentators disagree about whether it counts as “self-evolving”; the booklet reports no settled Commission position and recommends obtaining an early notified-body opinion. [f2091, f7436]

Separately, adding a brake command makes the function subject to the off-road functional-safety framework **ISO 19014**, using required Machine Performance Level (*MPLr*), rather than ISO 26262. The brake plant remains independently subject to **ISO 3450**. These technical obligations are distinct from resolving the ML classification. [f2071, f2855]

## Implications for approval timing

1. **Resolve classification and engage the assessor before the validation window.** The booklet warns that notified-body lead time alone could exceed its four-month validation window, but found **no published lead-time figure**. No pre-consultation by early 2027 is identified as an expert warning sign of a blocked regulatory route—not a statutory deadline. [f364, f259, f10786]
2. **Do not equate completed testing with completed conformity assessment.** EU acceptance runs through machinery conformity, and the booklet found no published commitment by an off-road regulator or notified body to accept virtual evidence. Assessor agreement on the evidence route is therefore a separate schedule dependency. [f2009, f258]
3. **Recheck standards immediately before the declaration of conformity.** The harmonised-standards list was still being prepared in 2026; the booklet explicitly calls for a standards-status checkpoint before the EU declaration. [f2092, f2867]

The defensible timing assumption is therefore **potential notified-body involvement for a 2027 launch, with unresolved assessment duration**, while separately tracking the 2028 AI requirements—not assuming ML braking is unregulated until 2028. [f2089, f2090, f2094, f259]

results.answer:
The most concrete published values come from **South Africa’s MOSH surface-mining industry specification**, rather than law. They are scenario-level engineering requirements—not a universal mining acceptance standard or a fleet-level reliability target. [f173, f2598, f2603]

## Concrete mining acceptance values

The booklet identifies these requirements in the **MOSH Surface Collision Prevention System Functional and Technical Performance Requirements, Rev 1**, with its fail-to-safe provisions. [f2113, f2607, f2359]

| Measure | Published acceptance value |
|---|---|
| Machine-to-machine detection range, surface operations | **200 m minimum**. [f2113] |
| Simultaneous tracking | **6 or more machines**. [f2606] |
| Position accuracy | **1.5 m or 10%, whichever is greater**. [f2607] |
| Warning before intervention | **2.5–3.0 seconds**. [f2115] |
| Stop gap at speeds **≤10 km/h** | **1.0–4.0 m**. [f2116] |
| Stop gap at speeds **>10 km/h** | **15 m ±5 m**. [f2117] |
| Fail-to-safe response | **Within 500 ms of detecting a critical failure**. This is not an obstacle-detection-to-braking latency requirement. [f2359] |
| False warnings and interventions at **TRL4** | **“No false interventions and false warnings”** at that test gate—not a published events-per-hour limit. [f2119, f2615, f2616] |

At TRL9, MOSH also requires **“no significant production loss”**, but the cited requirement supplies no numeric production-loss percentage. [f2614]

## What the standards and law add—and do not add

- **ISO 16001:2017:** detection time must be **≤300 ms**, but it covers object detection and warning, **not automatic braking**. It should not be treated as a complete intervention-system acceptance criterion. [f2064, f2070]
- **ISO 21815-3:** an exact public numeric pass table was **not found**. ISO 21815 and EMESRT PR-5A also do not supply a statistical acceptance target; the booklet recommends combining **PR-5A scenarios with MOSH’s numeric requirements**. [f2429, f324, f2646]
- **South African braking regulation:** specifies no detection percentage, distance, false-alarm limit or stopping-distance test. Mine acceptance is by the operator against the regulation, using industry guidelines as reference. [f2081, f1367]
- **US underground coal, 30 CFR 75.1732:** no numeric proximity-detection stopping distance; the proposed **3 ft** value was **not adopted**. [f2626]

## Important missing acceptance values

The booklet found **no published off-road acceptance value** for:

- Detection probability or miss rate. [f2620]
- False warnings per operating hour. [f2615]
- Unnecessary brake interventions per hour or per **1,000 hours**. [f2616]
- Availability or diagnostic coverage. [f2624]

Thus, **“zero false interventions at TRL4” is not evidence of a quantified field nuisance-braking rate**. The remaining fleet-level thresholds must come from the customer’s procurement or code-of-practice requirements and the programme’s acceptance specification—not be presented as ISO-mandated numbers. [f2119, f2603, f2598, f2636]

steps: evidence_brief {"question":"How hard can heavy off-road machines brake compared with cars, and how much does latency matter at 5–15 km/h?","max":20}
results.notes: Covers all five gold points with matching numbers and names. Calculated distances and the 59% illustration follow correctly from the cited equation. Useful planning caveats distinguish minimum requirements, commanded demand, measured capability, and machine-specific latency. Longer than necessary, but clear and well grounded.
results.answer:
**Heavy machines generally need lower braking assumptions than cars—but there is no single “heavy-machine maximum.” Latency matters enormously: at work-site speeds of 5–15 km/h, delay can account for half or more of the stopping distance.** [f5993, f5560, f6556, f144]

### How hard can they brake?

The booklet gives these useful benchmarks—not directly comparable measurements of maximum capability:

- **Cars:** UN R152 requires automatic emergency braking to *demand* at least **5.0 m/s²**. This is an on-road command requirement, not a guarantee of measured deceleration. [f5993]
- **Mining machines:** MOSH surface collision-prevention requirements specify emergency-stop deceleration of **1.9 m/s²** for machines whose top speed exceeds 20 km/h, and **1.0 m/s²** for other machines. [f5560]
- **US mining brake tests:** MSHA Table M-1 uses **2.94 m/s²** constant deceleration, with response time treated separately. [f5890, f13640]
- **NSW guidance:** proposed minimum net service-brake deceleration is **0.60 m/s² in service**, with grade and mass corrections. That is a proposed minimum—not an adopted rule or a machine’s maximum capability. [f13946]

So, **do not copy a car’s 5 m/s² assumption into a loader or haul-truck stopping model**. The definitions differ, and the booklet found no universal safe maximum automatic deceleration for earth-moving machinery. [f13640, f6556]

Nor is the explanation simply “they weigh more.” Mass cancels in an ideal friction-limited stopping model. Real machines face finite and thermally limited brake torque, payload-dependent axle loads and centre of gravity, severe slopes, deformable ground, and drivetrain braking. [f5887, f5888]

### How much does latency cost?

A simple allowance is:

\[
d_{\text{total}}=v\,t_{\text{delay}}+\frac{v^2}{2a}+d_{\text{clearance}}
\]

Here, \(a\) is the effective deceleration under the relevant conditions. The first term is distance travelled **before effective braking**. [f13648]

Calculated from that delay term, **each additional second costs**:

- At **5 km/h:** **1.39 m**
- At **10 km/h:** **2.78 m**
- At **15 km/h:** **4.17 m**. [f13648]

**Illustration—not a measured machine result:** at 10 km/h, assuming 1.0 m/s² constant deceleration and a 1-second delay, the machine travels **2.78 m during the delay**, then **3.86 m while braking**: **6.64 m total**, before clearance. At 5 km/h with the same assumptions, delay accounts for about **59%** of the stop. This illustrates the booklet’s conclusion that latency can dominate even at low speed. [f13648, f144]

### What delay should you assume?

Published examples vary substantially:

- **Under 0.3 s:** tracked-vehicle electro-hydraulic brake, 2026.
- **0.41 s:** mining electric-vehicle brake-by-wire, 2025.
- **0.5–2.5 s:** MSHA regulatory system-response assumptions by weight class.
- **1–2 s:** historic haul-truck retarder lag. [f5893, f5894, f5896, f5897]

These are different systems and definitions—not a measured fleet-wide latency range. **The booklet found no modern delay distributions for production wheel loaders, articulated haulers and haul trucks.** [f5899]

The practical recommendation—identified as expert opinion—is to use **measured latency, explicit brake build-up lag, and conservative deceleration for the actual grade, payload and surface**, rather than a generic car braking figure or an instantaneous-brake assumption. [f5905]

results.answer:
**Real field data exist, but the independent evidence is old and sparse.** The booklet’s strongest quantitative haul-truck evidence remains a NIOSH radar trial conducted in **2004**, published by T. M. Ruff in **2006**: **18% of alarms were false and 42% were nuisance alarms**. These are shares of recorded alarms—not rates per operating hour. [f101, f5173, f5174, f5175]

### The main measured field trial

Ruff’s *Evaluation of a radar-based proximity warning system for off-highway dump trucks*, in *Accident Analysis & Prevention* 38(1), 92–98, is independent, peer-reviewed evidence from a Caterpillar 793B at a US surface copper mine. [s266]

Over **seven days**, the radar alarm sounded during approximately **94% of 618 reverse movements**. The recorded alarms broke down as follows. [f3010]

| Alarm classification | Count | Share of 580 alarms |
|---|---:|---:|
| False: no significant object in the detection zone | 102 | 18% |
| Nuisance: real object, but no urgent danger in that task | 243 | 42% |
| Required immediate action or extra caution | 235 | About 41% |

The counts are the clearest figures: the booklet elsewhere reports the action-worthy share as 40%, versus 41% in its detailed count-based presentation. [f5174, f5175, f5176, f3011]

**The classification matters:**
- **False alarms** included responses to small ruts, rocks, foliage and dirt features rather than significant obstacles. [f3270]
- **Nuisance alarms** involved real objects the operator knew about and needed to approach—for example, backing toward a rock pile at a loading area. [f3271, f3272]
- **Dump-point berm detections were not classified as nuisance alarms**, even when the operator knew the berm was there, because overtravel could take the truck over an embankment. [f3273]

No missed detections were reported in that trial. Nevertheless, improving sensor precision alone would not have removed most unwanted alerts: interpreting the operating context was also necessary. [f3278, f3279]

### What happened to operator acceptance?

Drivers found the continuous audible warning annoying because most alarms did not signify danger, and researchers found the audible function disabled after shifts. This is direct field evidence of disengagement, although the disabling observation was partly anecdotal rather than a controlled behavioural endpoint. [f3280, f3281, x130]

There is also **qualitative counter-evidence**. In a Preco Preview radar trial on a Caterpillar 793B at **Phelps Dodge Morenci**, Ruff reported that occasional false alarms occurred, “but not frequently enough to cause the system to be ignored.” That observation does not supply a numerical acceptance threshold, but it prevents treating operator rejection as an inevitable result of any false alarms. [f7001] The source is NIOSH’s *Advances in Proximity Detection Technologies for Surface Mining Equipment*, circa 2004. [s676]

### What these data do—and do not—establish

- They document a substantial unwanted-alarm burden in an actual haul-truck operation, but **not a modern, fleet-wide performance benchmark**: the booklet explicitly characterizes independent off-road field data as old and sparse. [f101, f5173]
- **18% is not an acceptable-limit specification.** The observed problems do not establish that 17%, or even 5%, would be acceptable; nuisance frequency, urgency, alarm modality, operating phase and consequences all matter. [f3331]
- The booklet found **no published off-road acceptance values for false alarms per operating hour or unnecessary braking events per hour**. An Australian coal-industry project likewise left the acceptable false-alarm rate as an open research question. [f2121, f3019]
- It found no direct longitudinal mining studies measuring alarm fatigue physiologically or quantifying the probability of ignoring successive warnings. Annoyance and disabling are therefore better documented than a numerical “alarm-fatigue curve.” [f3304, f3305]

The key field lesson is the distinction between **detecting something that is not a significant obstacle** and **correctly detecting something that does not warrant a warning in the current task**. In the strongest measured trial, the second problem was larger. [f5174, f5175, f3279]

**Volvo CE, Caterpillar, Komatsu, Liebherr, John Deere, Epiroc and Sandvik already offer off-road automatic braking or stopping.** But the booklet’s October 2026 conclusion is that **every published operating envelope is narrow**—typically reverse/rear-zone operation, low speed, short brake pulses or tag-dependent detection. These are **vendor claims**; the research found no independent product-performance tests. [f1237, f1239, f1620, f1242]

The comparison below gives each manufacturer’s machines, intervention and published limits. “Automatic stopping” matters here: Komatsu’s motion-start intervention and Liebherr’s hydrostatic slowing are not equivalent to service-brake emergency braking during unrestricted travel. [f1642, f1648]

### Important qualifications

- **Volvo has the clearest numerical envelope:** the January 2023 system operates **in reverse at 3–15 km/h**, braking for **2–3 seconds**. The April 2025 announcement’s **0.5 km/h** threshold concerns *alerts*; it does not establish a wider automatic-braking band. [f1382, f1381, f1386, f1387]
- **Komatsu is not ongoing-swing collision avoidance.** KomVision stops at travel or swing start, not during an ongoing swing. It must be switched **off during trailer loading**, because a sudden stop can destabilize the machine. [f1642, f1646]
- **Caterpillar’s commercial dates need care.** Chapter 1 reports a **May 2025** wheel-loader launch, while Chapter 2 says the launch date was not found. Its forward-and-reverse asphalt-compactor system was shown in March 2026 and reported as slated for midyear launch—not confirmed shipped in the evidence reviewed. [f1068, f1632, f1071, f1636]
- **Missing environmental limits are not all-weather approval.** Published weather/light qualification, speed limits and false-intervention rates are incomplete or absent for several products. The evidence therefore does not establish unrestricted operation across dust, darkness, rain, snow and all site configurations. [f1650, f1639, f1656, f1671, f1695]

- **Linde Reverse Assist Radar**, if forklifts are in scope, slows in reverse and can stop; published limits and exclusions were not found. **Toyota SEnS+ should not be counted as automatic braking**: Toyota describes power-cut slowing, explicitly without braking to an automatic stop. - For **agricultural or forestry OEMs**, the booklet found no currently sold system combining documented object-triggered emergency braking with a public operating envelope. That is an evidence gap, not proof that no such product exists. [f1693]

results.answer:
**Yes—South Africa explicitly requires automatic slow-down and braking on certain mining machines.** The requirement has applied since **21 December 2022**; it was the only explicit mandate of this kind found by the booklet’s October 2026 review. [f164]

### South Africa: explicit automatic-braking requirement
Under **Mine Health and Safety Regulations 8.10.1.2(b) and 8.10.2.1(b)**, diesel-powered trackless mobile machines must detect a collision threat, warn, slow to a safe speed and then **apply the brakes automatically if the operator does not act**. The safety system must also “fail to safe without human intervention.” The regulations commenced through Government Gazette No. 47790, Notice 2908. [f2078, f2079, f2080]

The law itself does **not** specify a detection percentage, detection distance, false-alarm limit or stopping-distance test—a distinction between requiring the function and defining its quantitative acceptance criteria. [f2081]

### United States: a narrower automatic-stop requirement
There is an important qualification to “South Africa only”: **30 CFR 75.1732 (2015)** requires proximity-detection systems on continuous mining machines in **underground coal mines** to give audible and visual warnings and stop the machine before contacting a miner. That is a mandatory automatic-stop function, though not a general automatic-braking mandate for mining vehicles. [f2085, f2240]

So the precise answer is: **South Africa has the explicit mining-machine slow-down-and-braking mandate; the US also mandates proximity-triggered stopping for a specific class of underground coal-mining machine.** “Only jurisdiction found” describes the booklet’s research coverage, not proof that no other jurisdiction has any applicable requirement. [f164, f2240]

results.answer:
**No—not by replay alone.** Existing warning-system logs can validate perception and selected submodels, but they cannot validate the new closed-loop braking chain. [f7575]

### Where replay stops being valid
Replay feeds the software the recorded future regardless of its decisions. At the **first brake command that was absent from the original run**, that future no longer represents what the machine would have experienced. Replay can test when braking would have been triggered—not whether the resulting intervention would stop the machine safely. [f108, f109, f110]

### What the old logs can establish
- **Perception and trigger timing:** test detection, false alarms, warning timing and brake-trigger timing for the sensors, mounting positions and scenarios actually recorded. The booklet’s raw-sensor replay evidence here is vendor/on-road evidence. [f95, f109]
- **Candidate interventions:** cheaply estimate how often the new logic would have braked, in what circumstances, and its false-activation rate. [f10925]
- **Important limits:** existing logs are biased toward normal operation and shaped by operators’ reactions. Replay also does not retest hardware or influences upstream of the data-injection point, such as lenses, antennas, contamination, vibration or glare. [f7578, f96]

### What else is needed
Combine replay with **closed-loop simulation, hardware-in-the-loop and proving-ground tests** to evaluate braking consequences. The acceptance question must cover the complete sequence—detect, decide, intervene and stop with adequate margin—as well as unnecessary interventions, rather than merely whether a brake command was issued. [f110, f6982]

First audit whether the recordings are usable: replay needs raw sensor inputs, machine signals, accurate synchronized timestamps, calibration, labels and independent ground truth. The booklet did **not establish that the existing warning system retains these data**; insufficient fidelity or metadata should trigger stopping or escalation, not a validation claim. [f11899, f12991, f519, f10928]

Its qualification-gap discussion partially addresses the lack of an accepted realism score, but does not state the peer-reviewed sim-to-real domain-gap finding across sensors, especially in adverse weather; the narrower fog-mismatch example does not fully substitute for that point.
results.answer:
**Credible for selected effects within measured limits—not yet credible as stand-alone proof of all-weather off-road safety.** The booklet concludes that simulation can replace **part, but not most**, of physical sensor testing; published validation largely covers individual sensors and effects on road vehicles or in laboratories. [f4407, f4408]

### Fog: the strongest evidence, especially for lidar

Physics-based lidar models that include the complete sensor signal chain have matched real sensors closely in fog in several independent studies from **2021–2024**. This is **on-road evidence**, not proof of transfer to heavy off-road machines. [f5050]

The limits matter: agreement depends on matching the simulated and measured conditions, and model mismatch grew as fog visibility fell. In one physical fog-chamber test at **10 m visibility**, all lidars but one failed to detect a target at **10.5 m**—a reminder that accurately simulating degradation does not mean the real sensor remains adequate. [f7556, f7558, f7559]

### Dust: the biggest off-road gap

Lidar dust models exist, including a **2026 open-pit-mine framework** tuned to real mining lidar data, but their validation remains limited. Field measurements show **four distinct lidar behaviours in dust** that simple attenuation models miss. [f4424, f4425, f4426]

Dust also cannot safely be treated as merely “fog with a different colour”: machine-generated plumes depend on **machine speed, ground material and wind**. Representing them as static fog volumes can miss these relationships. [f5097]

The booklet searched for, but **did not find**, a validated **camera or radar dust model with a reported error metric**. Radar itself is substantially less affected by airborne dust and fog than cameras or lidar, but that physical robustness is not evidence that its simulation is validated. [f254, f5051]

### Snow: models exist, validation is weaker

Lidar snow models—including **LISA** and models by **Teufel et al.**—exist, but their validation is weaker than for fog and is based on **on-road evidence**. Radar snow attenuation also has less direct public validation than radar rain or fog attenuation. [f4630, f4634]

For **thermal and ultrasonic simulation**, the booklet found no adverse-weather or off-road validation. [f4435]

### What would make a simulation result trustworthy?

The booklet’s recommended test is **measured sensor and function behaviour—not visual realism**:

- **Correlate against physical measurements.** Adverse-environment models should be experimentally correlated; this is an expert recommendation, not an established off-road qualification standard. [f5219]
- **Check perception outcomes.** Compare real and simulated output distributions and downstream tasks, including detection and false-positive rates on real data, with confidence intervals for each weather-condition band. [f5057, f11102]
- **Declare the validated limits.** Record visibility, dust optical density, weather ranges, contamination and temperature rather than simply labelling a scene “dusty” or “snowy”. [f8009]
- **Do not assume transfer or combined-condition validity.** Different mounting heights, vibration, attachments and articulated bodies can invalidate on-road correlations; dense dust plus muddy covers and work lights plus airborne particles remain uncertain. [f5068, f5070]

**The central gap is qualification:** the booklet found neither an accepted method for qualifying off-road sensor models in dust, snow or fog nor off-road fidelity thresholds. Convincing generative weather edits do not close that gap—they are not yet trustworthy as test evidence on their own. [f331, f5220, f93]

results.answer:
**ISO 19014 is the applicable functional-safety framework for a brake-commanding function on earth-moving machinery—not ISO 26262.** Matching an existing warning system is insufficient because automatic braking is a different safety function, with different hazards and acceptance requirements. [f2071, f10417]

### Where the boundary lies
**ISO 19014-2** excludes awareness-only systems that do not affect machine motion. Once the system can command the brakes, it crosses into motion-affecting safety control: validation must address brake-command integrity, faults, degraded modes and unintended activation—not just detection accuracy. The series covers hardware, software and environmental testing. [f2075, f5223, f322]

### Why “as good as the old system” is the wrong target
- **The target must come from the new function’s hazard analysis.** ISO 19014-1 requires a machine-control-system safety analysis to determine the required risk reduction and corresponding required Machine Performance Level (**MPLr**). Equivalence to the old warning system does not establish that requirement. [f10516, f2071, f11989]
- **Both missed and inappropriate braking matter.** The booklet recommends separate analyses and acceptance thresholds for failure to intervene when needed, and intervention when unsafe or unnecessary. Matching warning performance does not settle either braking acceptance threshold. [f2141, f11987]
- **The old fleet remains useful evidence, not the acceptance criterion.** Its logs supply real off-road scenarios, approach speeds and false-alarm history; those inputs support validation, but the braking function still needs its own safety argument. [f5122, f6611, f11989]

**Edition caveat:** the booklet recommends rechecking the final publication status of revised ISO 19014-2 and ISO 19014-5 before design freeze. [f6286]

results.answer:
**Yes—but treat the recordings as the starting material for virtual sites, not as ready-made braking-validation environments.** The booklet finds camera and lidar logs useful for replay, real-site reconstruction and simulation near the recorded route; closed-loop testing needs substantial additional modelling. Most quantitative reconstruction evidence is **on-road**, not heavy off-road validation. [f3724, f3725, f3726]

## What you can build

- **Recorded-event replay:** rerun perception against what the sensors actually saw, measuring detection, false alarms and warning timing. This remains limited to the recorded sensors, mounting positions and scenarios; the cited replay evidence is vendor, on-road evidence. [f95]
- **Reconstructed sites:** recover real geometry and clutter, with neural reconstruction supplying appearance near the original viewpoints. These captures are useful as regression sites, incident reconstructions and anchors to reality. [f3701, f3703, f3753]
- **Editable, closed-loop sites:** extend the reconstruction with explicit geometry, collision shapes, sensor materials, controllable people and vehicles, and machine dynamics. That is an engineering conversion—not simply playing the recording inside a simulator. [f3726, f13151]

The booklet therefore recommends a **hybrid approach**: capture the real site for geometry and clutter, then use hand-built and procedural content for editability and systematic variations. This is its expert synthesis, rather than a demonstrated universal conversion pipeline. [f3700, f3701, f3702]

## What the conversion involves

1. **Qualify the logs:** synchronized cameras, lidar and motion/position sources—IMU, odometry or GNSS—with retained calibration and accurate poses. Existing recordings are not automatically suitable: only **50 of 200** sequences passed pose-quality checks in the on-road MV² dataset. [f3852, f3727]
2. **Reconstruct and clean:** build static geometry, register it to site coordinates, remove transient objects, classify terrain and objects, and explicitly repair unseen areas. [f13151]
3. **Make it testable:** add collision geometry and sensor materials, replace recorded people with controllable actors, and qualify the result against held-out measurements. [f13151]

Existing logging makes capture relatively inexpensive, but the booklet assesses processing and cleanup costs as **moderate to high**. [f3902]

## Where it breaks down

**1. Moving away from the recorded viewpoint.**  
Neural reconstruction degrades sharply at offsets of **1–4 m** in the cited on-road evidence; height changes are worse than sideways shifts, making transfer between different machine sensor heights particularly risky. There is no established universally safe mounting-change allowance. In Para-Lane, an image-reconstruction score fell from **22.99 to 17.05 dB** between the recorded and adjacent lanes. These are reconstruction results, not collision-mitigation performance results. [f81, f82, f4310, f3707]

**2. Poor capture geometry and difficult surfaces.**  
Photogrammetry fails predictably on textureless soil, reflections, glare, moving objects and pure camera rotation. Off-road preprints from 2026 add fine terrain detail, vibration-induced calibration drift and moving vegetation as degradation sources. [f3722, f3710]

**3. Recorded motion is not interactive behaviour.**  
A person captured walking through the scene is not automatically an actor whose timing or trajectory you can change. Captured moving objects are themselves a reconstruction problem; closed-loop braking requires controllable actors and machine dynamics beyond the recording. [f3884, f3726]

**4. Looking right is not sensing—or braking—right.**  
Camera appearance, lidar response, collision geometry, ground mechanics and machine dynamics are separate simulation layers. Lidar materials need wavelength-specific properties; visible appearance alone does not establish the required response. Camera/lidar reconstruction also does not automatically provide valid radar or ultrasonic testing. [f3712, f4298, f3724]

**5. A captured site is only one moment, not all seasons.**  
A capture freezes a particular site state. The booklet found no validated off-road camera or radar models for dust, snow and fog, and no evidence establishing heavy-machine braking-distance fidelity on loose and wet surfaces. Those are evidence gaps, not conditions that can be assumed valid after adding visual weather effects. [f3723, f3958, f4307]

## The practical boundary

Use reconstructed recordings as **real-site anchors and regression environments**, then add controlled variations rather than expecting an exact replica to cover everything. For future captures, the booklet recommends synchronized clocks, retained calibration, multiple passes and clear-weather mapping. [f3753, f3700, f3702, f13143]

Before virtual pass/fail results replace physical evidence, define each model’s **validity domain** and compare simulated versus measured sensor outputs, machine trajectories and braking outcomes. Validate task-level and closed-loop performance—not image similarity alone. [f4339, f4444]

The comparison below gives the dates, resources and deliverables. Three distinctions matter:

- **A method is not an approval.** PEGASUS’s 42-month, multi-company effort produced a validation method for one highway function—not a product approval. VVM then required a second four-year cycle for the next domain. [f1204, f1546, f1549]
- **Six months bought a pre-study.** VaViM—the booklet’s nearest precedent for transferring these methods to fenced-area/off-road vehicles—did not establish an accepted capability in six months. It concluded that validated models and real tests must be used side by side. [f1250, f1552, f1251]

steps: evidence_brief {"question":"What accident records say about fatal mechanisms for haul trucks and loaders, direction-specific runovers, driver deaths at berms/dump points, and
results.notes: All four gold claims are fully covered with matching numbers, equipment names and time periods. Additional detail is grounded in the supplied facts. The answer usefully distinguishes collision cases from victim counts, reversing statistics across equipment populations from loader-only statistics, and collision risks from berm and dump-point risks. It is longer than necessary but clear and useful for planning.
results.answer:
The records show two different collision patterns: **large haul trucks run forward over people or light vehicles they cannot see; smaller trucks and loaders commonly reverse over people.** But collisions are only part of the story: most haul-truck deaths in the booklet’s main US dataset involved berms and dump points, not hitting another person or vehicle. [f2995, f123]

### 1. Large haul trucks: forward run-overs, including starting from rest

In the NIOSH analysis of US surface-mine fatality reports from **January 2005–June 2021**, **12 of 13 fatal haul-truck collision cases involved forward movement**. Four began when the truck started moving with victims within **50 ft—about 15 m**. [f2990, f2991]

The detailed breakdown records five collisions involving light vehicles—including one double fatality—three involving pedestrians, three involving other haul trucks, and two involving other objects: a railroad car and a portable toilet. These are collision-case counts, not a clean victim count. [f3073]

The five light-vehicle cases make the mechanism particularly clear:
- Two trucks started forward from stationary.
- Two struck parked light vehicles in their path.
- One was a head-on interaction. [f3077]

Visibility is central: the booklet identifies a large machine running over a smaller vehicle or unseen person as the deadliest documented collision pattern. A **50-tonne haul truck can have a front-right blind area extending 18 m or more**. [f2983, f3589]

### 2. Loaders and smaller trucks: reversing over people

Among **22 US surface-mine blind-area deaths from 2000 to mid-2006**, dump trucks were involved in **38%** and front-end loaders in **33%**. Across that equipment population, **67% of victims were behind reversing equipment**. That 67% is not a loader-only statistic. [f2985, f2986]

So “reversing is the main danger” is population-specific: it fits the smaller-truck and loader pattern, but not the large-haul-truck collision cases above. Older research covering loader and haul-truck fatalities in **1995–2002** also identified **rollovers and pedestrian collisions** as the most common accident types. [f2995, f3092]

### 3. Truck drivers: loss of control, edges and ground failure

The broader haul-truck dataset classified **54 deaths** as:
- **21** involving berms;
- **12** at dump points;
- **13** in collisions;
- **8** from other causes. [f2989]

That puts berm and dump-point events at **33 of 54**, outweighing collisions. At the 12 fatal dump-point events, six trucks reversed over the edge and six involved ground failure; **10 had absent or inadequate berms**, and **seven drivers were unbelted**. These are overlapping circumstances, not separate death totals. [f2989, f2999, f3000, f3001]

A separate analysis of **133 US haul-truck-related fatalities, 1995–2010**, likewise found that drivers died mainly through loss of control, ground failure and two-vehicle collisions. Non-drivers died mainly through unexpected machine movement, falls from vehicles and being struck by other vehicles. [f3090, f3091]

### What the records do—and do not—establish

**A reverse-only warning system misses the characteristic large-haul-truck collision pattern; a people-and-vehicle detector misses much of the fatal risk to truck drivers at roadsides and dump edges.** [f2995, f3002]

These findings come principally from US mining records, not a worldwide, exposure-adjusted comparison. The booklet found no collision rates adjusted for hours or other exposure by machine type/model, and no worldwide breakdown of turning, swing and reversing collisions. The records therefore identify recurring ways people die; they do not establish which machine is intrinsically most dangerous per hour worked. [f3609, f3610]

results.answer:
The strongest objection is **“you have not yet earned the right to replace physical evidence”**, not “you need more simulated tests.” The next two are that **automatic braking needs a different safety acceptance target from warning**, and that sensor simulation is least credible in the conditions where failure matters most. [f10409, f10475, f10476, f10479]

This is a critique of the proposal described in the booklet, not a verified audit of your current plan: the research had no internal recordings, sensor specifications or project documents. [f7]

### Why these objections are hard to dismiss

- **Correlation can be circular.** A simulator tuned to reproduce its calibration tests has not demonstrated predictive performance on independent data. A reviewer will also question whether the simulator and the test oracle—the mechanism deciding whether a result passes—share assumptions that could reproduce the same error. [f8159, f10233]
- **Better detection is not enough.** Braking is a new safety-control function, with hazards from unintended intervention as well as missed intervention. As a concrete, **vendor-only** precedent, Komatsu advises switching off stop control on slopes, slippery or soft ground, with suspended loads and when loading trailers. [f10476, f10420]
- **The schedule lacks a demonstrated precedent.** The booklet found no case, in any industry, of a new automatic braking function progressing from first representative hardware to accepted validation in about **four months**. Every documented reduction in physical testing rested on years of prior investment, a deliberately narrow operating envelope, or both. That does not prove the deadline impossible; it makes an unconditional commitment difficult to defend. [f58, f59]

The checklist below gives all ten objections in the booklet’s priority order. That ordering reflects how directly each attacks the proposal, evidence strength and off-road relevance, and how difficult late recovery would be—not measured probabilities of failure. [f10472]

### Three changes that would most increase reviewer confidence

1. **Make physical-test substitution claim-specific.** Produce a one-page credibility map linking each safety claim to virtual, physical or mixed evidence; the real data validating its model; remaining uncertainty; and the person authorized to accept it. Seek approval for particular substitutions, rather than blanket approval of “virtual validation.” [f10907, f11154]

2. **Put a blind credibility gate before scale-up.** Reserve independent physical data that cannot be used for tuning, agree acceptance metrics before results are seen, and demonstrate that model uncertainty does not dominate the safety conclusion. Retain physical confirmation of the highest-risk cases. The booklet proposes a **March–April 2027** gate requiring a blind pilot, assessor feedback, a P80 completion date inside the deadline, and an independent decision to proceed, restrict scope or fall back; that timing is a planning recommendation, not demonstrated delivery evidence. [f8159, f11114, f11124, f10198]

3. **Protect a restricted-scope fallback now.** Secure supplier data and rights, capture winter evidence while available, and obtain early conformity and legal feedback on the intended substitutions. Keep a costed fallback instead of assuming physical tests—and their costs—will disappear. Machinery-regulator acceptance of simulation evidence was **not found**, so the on-road precedents cannot settle that question for you. [f10485, f10493, f10960, f11156, f11188]

### The reviewer’s ten strongest challenges—in booklet priority order

- [ ] 1. Why should we trust the simulator enough to retire physical tests? — Show independent physical correlation, uncertainty and an approved validity envelope—not just virtual run counts. [f10475, f8060]
- [ ] 2. Are we validating automatic braking, or merely matching the old warning system? — Treat missed and unintended intervention as safety hazards; trace safety requirements to virtual, HIL and machine evidence. [f10476, f11095]
- [ ] 3. Where is the real evidence for adverse-condition sensing? — Dust, fog, snow, rain, glare and darkness are precisely the weak points in sensor-model credibility. [f10479]
- [ ] 4. Why should one machine’s validation transfer to another? — Retain physical brake tests and representative surface/grade anchors; adequate terramechanics validation for braking prediction was not found. [f10481, f10482, f10484, f11117]
- [ ] 5. Are supplier data, rights and prototype configuration actually secured? — Missing supplier artifacts can block testing; prototype changes can invalidate assumed models. The latter is an inference from V&V practice. [f10485, f10488, f10489]
- [ ] 6. What makes four months a forecast rather than a wish? — No comparable first-hardware-to-accepted-validation precedent was found. Winter 2026–27 is the last northern cold-season data opportunity for this window. [f58, f10490, f10493]
- [ ] 7. Will nuisance stops create hazards or get the system disabled? — Require operational evidence, not detection performance alone; disabling and workarounds are documented risks. [f10495]
- [ ] 8. Who has agreed to accept this evidence for conformity and liability purposes? — Machinery acceptance of simulation evidence was not established; applicability to frozen ML remains contested. Obtain assessor and counsel feedback early. [f11188, f11212, f10960]
- [ ] 9. Does the campaign demonstrate coverage, or merely count scenarios? — Show hazard and boundary coverage; benchmark end-to-end delivery rather than treating simulation volume as proof. [f218, f10260, f10161]
- [ ] 10. Are savings being booked before physical-test substitution is approved? — Identify test categories actually approved for retirement and maintain a costed fallback. [f219, f11154, f11156]

results.answer:
**Prefer a hybrid—not a fully bespoke open-source build or an unquestioned commercial “complete solution.”** For an organization starting from zero, the booklet recommends owning the validation knowledge internally, licensing or co-developing machine physics, and using a specialist partner for the first sensor model correlated against physical measurements. This is **expert judgment**, not a proven cost or schedule winner. [f201, f199]

### When each option makes sense

- **Lean commercial when reducing integration burden is the priority.** Integrated suites reduce interfaces and support work, but machine-specific modeling and correlation against real measurements remain substantial internal tasks. Buying the software does not buy validated off-road realism. [f9359, f8748, f16170]
- **Lean open source when you can sustain the integration engineering.** Someone must build and maintain the coupling, assets, scenario database and validation evidence. The booklet’s open-source-core example also requires major work for validated radar, physics-based ultrasonic sensing and weather effects backed by correlation evidence; scarce specialist skills are a constraint. [f8303, f16161]
- **Lean hybrid when you need outside specialization without surrendering long-term control.** The booklet judges an internal owner plus a partner and commercial or open-source components to offer the best balance—provided ownership clauses are unusually clear. [f16134]

### What to retain in-house

Keep the **operating-domain definition, scenario catalog, acceptance criteria and correlation data** under your control. Buy specialist implementation where useful, but require clear ownership terms and **open-format export** to limit lock-in and supplier-consolidation risk. [f16125, f16134, f13217]

### Compare total cost, not license price

Open source still carries substantial engineering and maintenance costs. The booklet estimates a labor floor of roughly **USD 150,000–260,000 per specialist per year**, meaning even free-software programs can cost seven figures annually. These are planning figures, not a quotation for your team. Commercial budgets must come from vendor quotations. [f8303, f13550, f13551, f8308]

### The decisive purchase criterion

**Choose for evidence credibility, not feature breadth.** No single commercial or open-source tool has public evidence of validating heavy off-road automatic braking across many job-site types and all-weather sensing. Nor did the booklet find a public off-highway build-versus-buy study establishing team size, timeline or total cost. A commercial stack may reduce integration effort; neither route eliminates physical correlation work. [f200, f8281, f199, f8748]

So the defensible default is: **own the validation capability; buy or partner for difficult components; use open source selectively where your team can maintain and substantiate it.** [f201, f16134]

results.answer:
**No—a fixed time-to-collision (TTC) threshold is not good enough as the primary brake trigger at work-site speeds.** The booklet recommends deciding from **predicted stopping distance and the collision-risk zone**, with TTC as a supporting input. [f148, f149]

### Why TTC alone fails
The booklet identifies several physical limitations:
- Near zero closing speed, TTC becomes enormous or unstable even when someone is centimetres from the machine. [f6214]
- A stationary machine about to move presents a start-up hazard for which TTC is undefined. [f6219]
- Articulation, excavator swing and track counter-rotation can cause collisions without longitudinal closing speed. [f6218]
- Grade, mud, payload, brake condition and turning change the safe intervention point—so the same TTC does not imply the same stopping capability. [f5818]

### What should determine the braking moment?
Use the distance remaining **along the predicted collision path**, compared with everything the machine needs before it can stop safely. The booklet proposes this practical stopping-margin calculation:

\[
M=R-(D_\text{perception}+D_\text{decision}+D_\text{action}
+D_\text{stop,predicted}+D_\text{safe})
\]

Here, \(R\) is path distance to the collision point; the other terms cover distance consumed by sensing, decision and actuator delays, predicted braking, and final clearance. This implementation is **expert opinion**, consistent with the ISO stopping-distance structure—not a prescribed universal algorithm. [f6208, f6114]

The decision should then work as follows:

- **Adapt the stopping envelope to machine state:** speed, grade, traction, load, brake/drive state and steering or articulation—not just object range. [f6114, f5818]
- **Escalate intervention as the stopping margin is consumed.** Calibrate the transition from partial to full braking using the remaining margin **and its uncertainty**, rather than range alone. Full-stop or maximum-safe mitigation braking is typically needed when the available distance approaches stopping distance plus clearance and a collision would otherwise be unavoidable. [f6280, f6515]
- **Limit braking to what the machine can safely deliver.** The booklet’s synthesis recommends the lesser of the deceleration needed to avoid collision and that allowed by stability, brake capacity and payload, with a limit on how abruptly deceleration changes—jerk. [f152]
- **Do not cancel intervention just because the operator touched a control.** The booklet recommends reducing or suppressing it only when the operator’s resulting trajectory is at least as safe as the automatic action. [f6342]

The booklet describes ISO 21815-3:2023 as placing intervention at **collision-risk level 4 or above**; that is a risk-level requirement, not a universal TTC value. [f5912]

### How to establish the actual thresholds
Tune and test families of conflict scenarios across the **whole sensor-to-actuator chain**, balancing collision avoidance against unnecessary braking. That validation process is transferable from road practice; the numerical thresholds are not automatically transferable. Before live brake actuation, the booklet recommends shadow-mode trials and site-specific review of hypothetical interventions, including false stops during ordinary work. [f6195, f10729]

**There is no defensible universal “brake at X seconds” value in the booklet:** it found no standard or peer-reviewed study supplying tuned off-road TTC or deceleration values. It also found no head-to-head off-road study proving distance-and-zone logic superior to TTC alone—the recommendation rests on the standards structure and engineering reasoning, not comparative field proof. [f5916, f6224, f6572]

Estimate this as a **probabilistic, evidence-gated programme**, not a single promised finish date. Present executives with **P50 and P80 completion dates plus the probability of meeting the fixed deadline**—all calculated from the programme’s own schedule model. [f9439, f9640]

### How to estimate it

1. **Start with actual history.** Reconstruct what consumed the previous three-to-four-year effort: that determines whether virtual validation addresses the real bottleneck. For new work, use comparable component-level histories—model development, supplier deliveries, toolchain commissioning, data preparation, correlation campaigns and safety reviews—rather than assuming a comparable complete programme exists. Reference-class forecasting is credible only when the comparisons are genuinely similar; this component-decomposition approach is a recommendation, not a separately validated forecasting method. [f273, f9439, f9437, f9616]

2. **Build one integrated dependency schedule.** Make duration assumptions, critical and near-critical paths, long-lead items, external dependencies and integration buffers explicit. A deterministic plan is particularly optimistic where several parallel workstreams must all finish before the next milestone. [f10171, f10244, f10245, f9633]

3. **Put uncertainty where it actually exists.** Assign duration ranges and simulate the dependency network using Monte Carlo analysis. Include uncertainty in model accuracy, data access, hardware delivery, integration, safety review and rework; explicitly model prototype slippage and pessimistic model-to-test correlation outcomes. Separate uncertainty from contingency—blanket “add 20%” padding is not defensible—and protect the first physical-correlation test with a buffer. [f16324, f9642, f10377, f11155, f9641, f9650]

4. **Calculate confidence for both preparation and delivery.** P50 is the date by which half the simulated schedules finish; P80 is the date by which 80% finish. Also calculate the share finishing by the externally fixed deadline. These figures cannot be inferred from the booklet or assigned by executive preference. [f16327, f9640]

### How to present it

Use the executive brief structure below. The main schedule visual should be a **completion-probability S-curve marked with P50, P80 and the deadline**, or milestone confidence windows—not exact-date bars alone. Pair it with a **schedule-sensitivity tornado chart** showing which task uncertainties move the finish date most. Keep the integrated schedule and basis of estimate available for audit. [f9889, f16328, f10171]

A suitable headline template is:

> “For the stated scope, the current model gives a P50 completion date of **[date]**, a P80 date of **[date]**, and a **[percentage]** probability of meeting **[deadline]**.”

These are placeholders until the programme model produces them. [f9640, f16327]

### The caveat executives must hear

**Four months is a target, not an established forecast.** The research found no case of a new automatic-braking function progressing from first representative hardware to accepted validation in about four months. The booklet’s proposed route is to move substantial preparation ahead of prototype arrival—not to assume simulation makes that work disappear. [f10464, f58, f62]

Make commitment conditional on evidence. In the booklet’s illustrative cadence, the **March–April 2027 readiness gate** requires a successful blind pilot, assessor feedback, a P80 date inside the deadline and independent judgment on readiness, restricted scope or fallback. Pre-agree go, restrict, pivot and stop criteria, and fund a costed restricted-scope fallback in parallel rather than protecting the headline date by weakening the evidence requirement. [f10198, f9449, f10747]

### Executive schedule brief — first two pages

- [ ] Decision and scope — Decision requested; why now; what will and will not exist by the deadline. [f9854]
- [ ] Forecast, not just target — Preparation and delivery confidence windows; completion S-curve with P50/P80 and probability of meeting the fixed deadline. [f9889, f9439]
- [ ] What drives the date — Critical and near-critical paths, integration buffer, long-lead items and least-controllable external dependency. Add a sensitivity tornado chart. [f10244, f10245, f16328]
- [ ] Downside and fallback — Show pessimistic correlation impacts, descoping steps and a costed restricted-scope fallback funded in parallel. [f11155, f9649, f10747]
- [ ] Leadership action — Resources and decisions required; evidence-gate criteria, named decider and go/restrict/pivot/stop options. [f9854, f9449]

results.notes: All five gold gaps are stated explicitly and accurately. Additional gaps are grounded in the supplied facts, and the answer translates them into useful internal measurement, validation and acceptance tasks. It correctly distinguishes absence of published evidence from proof that private evidence does not exist. Longer than necessary, but clearly organized and useful for planning.
results.answer:
The biggest missing pieces are **evidence that the simulator is trustworthy, real machine-and-operator performance data, and agreement on what evidence will be accepted**. The booklet treats these as questions for the manufacturer, supplier requests or early experiments—not assumptions to fill with borrowed numbers. “Not found” means not found in published sources, not that the evidence cannot exist privately. [f263]

## 1. What counts as an acceptable result
The research found **no off-road regulator or notified body committing to accept virtual evidence**, and no evidence establishing whether the test procedures in ISO 16001, ISO 21815-1 or ISO 21815-3 accept simulation. Nor is there a universal permitted percentage of virtual testing or universal simulation-error tolerance. [f258, f11192, f187]

**We need to establish:** agreement with the relevant reviewers on acceptance criteria, simulation credibility and the physical tests that must remain. Matching the old warning system is not sufficient: automatic braking is a different safety function. [f275, f10417]

For machine-learning perception, notified-body lead times were not found; whether a frozen, non-learning model triggers the Machinery Regulation’s particular notified-body route also remains unresolved by notified-body evidence. These need direct clarification rather than schedule assumptions. [f259, f11187]

## 2. How our machines actually stop
The booklet found no published modern **brake-delay distributions** for production wheel loaders, articulated haulers or haul trucks; no validation of simulated heavy-machine stopping distance on gravel, mud, ice or slopes; and no off-road case comparing simulation-tuned braking thresholds with field results. [f252, f253, f251]

**We need to establish:** measured delays and stopping performance for our machines and conditions, followed by physical checks that simulation-selected intervention thresholds work in reality. These are evidence gaps, not merely missing model parameters. [f252, f253, f251, f263]

## 3. Whether sensor simulation works in the difficult conditions
No validated radar or camera dust model with a reported error metric was found. The research also found no off-road sensor-model fidelity thresholds, no validated vibration-to-sensor-output model, and no adverse-weather or off-road validation for thermal or ultrasonic simulation. [f254, f5220, f4431, f4435]

**We need to establish:** sensor-specific agreement against real measurements, with explicit error limits and a declared range of conditions in which each model can be trusted—not simply realistic-looking scenes. [f187, f275]

## 4. Operator response and tolerable nuisance intervention
The research found no published representative reaction times to proximity warnings, no validated off-road operator model, no operator-accepted false-alarm rate, and no published off-road values for false alarms or unnecessary braking **per operating hour**. [f247, f250, f248, f249]

**We need to establish:** our operational baseline, actual warning-response behavior, and acceptable nuisance-warning and nuisance-braking limits. There is no published off-road benchmark here that we can simply adopt. [f247, f248, f249, f263]

## 5. What constitutes sufficient coverage
No published method or standard sets the required number of virtual environments. Exposure distributions across the proposed **100+ site types** were also not found. [f255, f1115]

**We need to establish:** which conditions and encounters matter for our intended use, how frequently they occur, and why the selected environments represent them. A site or scenario count alone cannot resolve these missing inputs. [f255, f1115]

## 6. What evidence transfers between machines
The booklet found no published approach for transferring perception evidence across sensor mounting positions, no published off-road variant-transfer example, and no ISO rule saying that testing a fixed number of representative machines validates the whole family. No case quantified the time saved by reusing evidence across machine models. [f260, f7574, f6683, f261]

**We need to establish:** which variants are genuinely similar, what changes invalidate earlier evidence, and what additional physical evidence is needed for each extension. We cannot assume that validation transfers with the software. [f260, f6683, f263]

## 7. Whether the promised schedule and savings are real
No published effort, cost, team-size or timeline figures were found for building job-site environments or an off-highway virtual-validation capability. The research also found no public off-road manufacturer statement that simulation, replay or hardware-in-the-loop shortened validation, and **no case in any industry** of a new automatic-braking function reaching accepted validation about **four months** after first representative hardware. [f256, f257, f58]

**We need to establish:** our own measured delivery effort and savings, and why the previous comparable validation took **three to four years**—the research found no published explanation of that history. The business case cannot treat the proposed compression as an established precedent. [f262, f256, f58]

## An immediate internal gap
The research used **no internal recordings, sensor specifications, site video or documents**. Machine types, sensor types, software maturity and existing recordings were unknown. Establishing what we already possess is therefore distinct from commissioning new research or tests—and should come first when deciding how large these gaps actually are. [f7, f8, f263]

results.notes: Clear, well-grounded guidance covering paired recording, common world/risk coordinates, and the invalidity of raw sensor comparisons. The metrics claim is partial because interventions per hazard are omitted, although warnings per hazard, missed hazards, hourly false/nuisance alarms, TTC, common ground truth, and the ISO 21815-3 risk area are included. The separate treatment of braking safety requirements is supported and useful.
results.answer:
Compare **responses to the same real-world hazards—not raw sensor outputs**. Use the old system as the baseline for the common detection/warning stages, but assess the new braking function against its own hazard-derived safety requirements, not simply “better than the old system.” [f105, f107, f111, f10529]

### 1. Give both systems the same encounters
The booklet’s preferred experiment is to record both sensor suites **simultaneously on the same machine**, preserving their intended mounting geometry and checking them against an independent reference trajectory. This is an expert recommendation; separate deployments introduce site, operator and weather differences. Also test whether co-mounting creates occlusion or electromagnetic/optical interference. [f5509, f5482, f5511]

### 2. Use a common safety yardstick
Define hazards using a shared world-coordinate risk zone—for example, the **ISO 21815-3 risk area**—rather than each sensor’s native field of view. Measure distance from the machine’s relevant swept envelope, not the sensor origin: otherwise mounting position can change the apparent warning range without changing the safety margin. [f106, f5501]

Against that common ground truth, compare:
- Warnings per hazard and missed hazards.
- False and nuisance alarms **per hour under equal exposure**.
- Warning timing relative to hazard-zone entry, time to collision or distance. [f5478]

Ground-truth accuracy matters: poorly calibrated reference measurements can produce verdict errors larger than the differences between systems. [f7474]

### 3. Keep sensor performance and decision logic separate
Do **not** directly compare raw detections, confidence scores or per-sensor statistics when modality, mounting or processing differs. Compare encounter-level outcomes instead. Old raw logs are not valid inputs representing a new sensor or mounting position. [f107, f5477, f5512]

For a separate decision-logic test, common object lists can remove sensor differences—but that assumes perception has succeeded and can hide latency, occlusion, false detections and range/classification errors. It is therefore not an end-to-end perception comparison. [f5259]

### 4. Give braking its own verdict
The old warning-only system has no braking function to benchmark. Compare the shared warning stage with the baseline; evaluate braking against the new safety requirements rather than treating stopping performance as an old-versus-new metric. [f5445, f10529]

**Bottom line:** use a paired, common-ground-truth comparison to judge detection and warning improvements; use a separate safety assessment to establish whether automatic braking is acceptable. Those are different claims, and neither substitutes for the other. [f105, f5445, f10529]

The other gold claims are covered.
results.answer:
**ISO 21815 is the core off-road collision-warning and avoidance standard family**, covering earth-moving, mobile underground-mining and road-construction machinery. It addresses object detection, operator warnings, automatic intervention and testing; the family is still being completed. [f2055, f381]

### Coverage and status by part

The statuses below are those recorded in the **October 2026 booklet**, not a live catalogue check.

| Part | What it covers | Status recorded in the booklet |
|---|---|---|
| **ISO 21815-1:2022** | **General requirements** for detection, warnings, automatic intervention and test procedures. | **Published.** [f2056] |
| **ISO/TS 21815-2:2021** | **On-board J1939 communication interface** between the collision-warning/avoidance system and the machine. | **Published Technical Specification**, confirmed in **December 2024**. [f2057] |
| **ISO 21815-3:2023** | **Risk area and risk level for forward/reverse motion.** | **Published.** [f2058] |
| **ISO 21815-4** | **Risk area and risk level for swing and rotation motion.** Its approach is primarily to inhibit motion before rotation starts, rather than brake during rotation. | **Stage 60.00, “Under publication,” since 4 September 2026**, with first-edition publication scheduled for **October 2026**. The booklet explicitly warns against citing it as published until the text appears. [f2059, f3379, f2170, f1708, f2172] |
| **ISO/PRF 21815-5** | **Risk area and risk level for other forms of motion**: articulation, four-wheel steering, reversing towed trailers, differential/skid-steer turning, telescopic extension/retraction and vertical height/depth movements. | **Proof stage 50.20 since 9 September 2026**, with publication expected in **November 2026**. Its final-draft ballot was approved on **25 June 2026**; it was not yet recorded as published. [f2176, f10904, f2671] |

### Important boundaries

- **Collision avoidance does not mean autonomous steering:** Part 1 limits intervention to speed reduction, stopping or motion inhibition—not automatic steering. Part 5’s inclusion of steering-related movements concerns collision risks caused by those movements, not automatic evasive steering. [f5909, f2176]
- **The motion-specific parts divide the scope:** Part 3 handles forward/reverse travel, Part 4 swing/rotation, and Part 5 other movements. [f2177]
- **It is not a simulation-credibility standard:** the booklet found that ISO 21815 does not specify how to prove a simulation credible. [f4411]

For a current compliance baseline, **verify Parts 4 and 5 in the ISO catalogue** rather than treating their scheduled publication dates as proof of publication. [f2172, f55]

results.answer:
**Simulation becomes credible safety evidence when physical tests demonstrate its predictive accuracy for a specific safety claim, within a declared operating envelope, with quantified uncertainty and independent review. There is no defensible universal percentage of testing that must remain physical:** physical tests establish the anchors; simulation fills the validated interior; physical confirmation remains at boundaries and after influential changes. [f186, f187, f7536]

## What would make the results acceptable?

1. **Agree the claim and acceptance route first.** Identify who will accept the evidence, and specify exactly which machine, sensors, mounting, software and environmental conditions it covers. Approve specific substitutions—“this validated model replaces this repetitive test within this envelope”—rather than approving “virtual testing” wholesale. [f1987, f10910]

2. **Validate against independent measurements, not tuning data.** Keep calibration, validation and withheld confirmation datasets separate. Matching a test used to tune the model does not demonstrate predictive capability on new data. A strong pilot predicts a deliberately difficult, narrow end-to-end case blind, against criteria registered beforehand. [f193, f8159, f9485]

3. **Demonstrate the whole safety chain.** Validation must cover the same system boundary as the claim. Separately validated perception and brake models do not remove the need for integrated closed-loop tests; where J1939 is used, end-to-end integration latency must be included. Matching the old warning system is insufficient because automatic braking is a different safety function. [f8195, f8197, f8198, f10417]

4. **Use decision-relevant metrics and uncertainty bounds.** Assess several measures together—safety-quantity errors, time histories and distribution-level agreement—not one overall score. There is no universal allowable simulation-to-test error. Set program-specific limits for false alarms and unnecessary brake events, and test hazardous unintended braking as well as failure to brake. [f188, f7553, f187, f180, f8203]

5. **Provide an auditable credibility dossier.** The checked frameworks expect verification, risk-scaled validation effort and independent review. Report best estimates, uncertainty, factor-by-factor credibility, validity limits and failed validation cases—not just successful runs. [f186, f193]

**Credible does not automatically mean accepted for machinery conformity.** The booklet found no public text in ISO 21815, ISO 17757 or ISO 19014 defining when simulation evidence is acceptable, nor evidence establishing acceptance by a machinery regulator or notified body. Full paid standards were not checked, so “not found” is not proof of prohibition. [f8321, f11188, f7544]

## What physical testing should remain?

The booklet’s recommended retained set is:

- **Braking:** physical brake-performance and stopping-distance tests for each machine class across load, slope and surface extremes. ISO 3450 requires physical brake-performance testing. [f7881, f10431]
- **Detection and unintended intervention:** ISO 21815-1 clause 6 performance and false-positive tests per scenario class. This retained-test split is an expert recommendation. [f7884]
- **Difficult sensing conditions:** characterization at mounting-geometry extremes and in degraded visibility, particularly dust, darkness and glare. HIL and physical tests remain important for poorly modelled electronics, timing, soiling, vibration, metal clutter and heavy rain. [f7885, f4972]
- **Full-system confirmation:** assessor-selected end-to-end runs, including at least one per EMESRT scenario family, plus closed-loop tests at the collision/no-collision boundary. These are booklet recommendations, not universal regulatory minima. [f7887, f7888]
- **Changes and discrepancies:** new phenomena, smallest-margin conditions, unexplained simulation errors and influential configuration changes. A new machine variant needs bridging evidence; even within the validated parameter range, the recommendation includes reduced physical brake calibration and sensor field-of-view/detection checks. [f7850, f189, f7917]

The conservative interpretation is to **retain prescribed physical tests unless the applicable document explicitly permits substitution**. [f2486]

## How many tests—or what percentage?

**No universal number is supported.** Every documented reduction depended on years of earlier simulation/statistical investment, a deliberately narrow operating envelope, or both. [f187, f59]

Two numerical examples must not be mistaken for approval thresholds:

- **10–30 physical points** is the booklet’s suggested credibility-pilot size—not a complete validation campaign. [f9917]
- **At least 10 latency repetitions across oil temperatures per machine family** is an early physical-test recommendation—not a total test minimum. [f13685]

The often-cited **30% physical minimum** comes from an on-road UTAC CERAM working document and vendor interpretation. The booklet instead identifies the WP.29 text of **28 August 2025** as leaving confirmation-test counts to manufacturer–authority agreement; none of these establishes an off-road percentage. [f7547, f7548, f7549]

The defensible decision is therefore **test-by-test substitution within a proven envelope**, not a target such as “70% virtual.” [f10910, f187]

The count-reconciliation caveat is supported by retrieved fact f15607 as well as the cited distinction in f6234. Additional acceptance and integration cautions are supported and useful for a planner.
results.answer:
**EMESRT PR-5A provides two complementary things: scenarios describing how mining vehicles and people can collide, and nine layers of control to prevent those interactions. Automatic braking belongs at Level 9—intervention—not Level 8, which only warns the operator.** [f317, f5924]

## Vehicle-interaction scenarios

PR-5A represents surface-mining interactions as **Functional Performance Scenario Storyboards**—descriptions of hazardous situations against which a system can be assessed. The families described in the booklet include: [f7746, f15606]

- Following another vehicle on straight roads and curves.
- Overtaking.
- Head-on encounters.
- Interactions at junctions.
- Congested dump and parking areas.
- Light vehicles interacting with heavy equipment. [f15606]

The booklet also gives “vehicle reversing towards a person” as an example of an EMESRT functional scenario. [f6736]

**The counts need care:** a 2019 trade article reports **24 scenarios**, while EMESRT’s 2024 Activity Report refers to **17 published surface storyboards**. One chapter interprets these as different things—defined scenarios versus published storyboards—but the booklet does not consistently reconcile them. They should not be presented as interchangeable counts or as a verified complete list here. [f319, f320, f6234]

## The nine levels of control

PR-5A names the levels as follows. They are layers of defense, with awareness, warnings and intervention sitting above the site’s underlying controls. [f4080, f15604]

| Level | Control |
|---|---|
| **1** | Site Requirements |
| **2** | Segregation Controls |
| **3** | Operating Procedures |
| **4** | Authority to Operate |
| **5** | Fitness to Operate |
| **6** | Operating Compliance |
| **7** | Operator Awareness |
| **8** | Advisory Controls—warn the operator |
| **9** | Intervention Controls—automatically slow or stop the machine |

[f4080, f15604]

## Where automatic braking fits

The distinction is **who acts**: Level 8 advises the operator; at Level 9 the system takes control from the operator to slow or stop the machine. Automatic collision-mitigation braking is therefore a Level 9 capability. [f15604, f4081]

That does **not** mean fitting automatic braking replaces the earlier controls. EMESRT/ICMM guidance says effective Level 8–9 implementation first requires understanding the effectiveness of the **Level 1–7 baseline**, and intervention technology must be integrated with existing site controls. The booklet consequently warns against validating braking in isolation from roadway design, segregation, procedures and advisory controls. [f702, f704, f15611]

Finally, **“Level 9” is not proof of safety or acceptance**. EMESRT’s framework is industry risk-control guidance, not law, and it does not demonstrate that a product passes a particular mine’s acceptance test. PR-5A also supplies no statistical acceptance target: the scenario framework and intervention label do not, by themselves, establish how much testing is enough. [f2586, f2587, f324]
